                [32m'## Background\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'`/home/user/pricing-audit` is an already-initialized Gel project. A local Gel server (version `6.11`) is installed in this container with its data directory already bootstrapped, and the `gel` CLI is on `PATH` with all connection settings preconfigured through the environment, so plain `gel query ...` / `gel migrate` calls work from any directory once the server is up.                 [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'The current schema (`dbschema/default.gel`) declares a single object type `default::Product` with `sku` (exclusive), `name`, `price_cents` and `stock`. One migration (`dbschema/migrations/00001-*.edgeql`) has been created and applied, and the database already holds 8 seeded products.\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m"The pricing team keeps discovering price edits that nobody can explain, because bookkeeping currently lives in whichever application happens to touch the database. They want an audit subsystem that **cannot be bypassed**: the audit records and the bookkeeping fields must be produced by the database itself, so that even a raw `gel query 'update Product ...'` is recorded. You must build the whole thing with Gel SDL, the migration workflow and EdgeQL through the `gel` CLI — do **not** write any Python, TypeScript, Go or other client-library code.\n"[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'## Requirements\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'### 1. Bookkeeping fields on `Product`\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'Extend `default::Product` (keep the existing properties and constraints intact) with two required properties that the database maintains on its own:\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'- `revision: int64` — a new product starts at `1`. Every `update` statement that matches the product increases its `revision` by exactly `1`, **even when the statement does not actually change any value**.\n'[39m +
                [32m'- `price_history: array<int64>` — a product inserted after your change starts with `[<its price_cents>]`. Every `update` that changes `price_cents` appends the new price to the array; an `update` that leaves `price_cents` at its current value must leave the array untouched.\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'The 8 products that already exist must be backfilled with `revision = 1` and `price_history = []` (do not synthesize history for them).\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'### 2. `default::AuditEvent` — one append-only row per audited row change\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'Properties:\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'- `action: str`, required, restricted to exactly the values `insert`, `update`, `delete`.\n'[39m +
                [32m'- `sku: str`, required.\n'[39m +
                [32m'- `old_price_cents: int64`, optional.\n'[39m +
                [32m'- `new_price_cents: int64`, optional.\n'[39m +
                [32m'- `recorded_at: datetime`, required, defaulting to the time of the statement that created it.\n'[39m +
                [32m'- `summary: str`, required, and **always derived by the database from the other properties of the same object when the row is inserted** (a caller-supplied value must never survive). Exact formats:\n'[39m +
                [32m"  - `action = 'insert'` → `INSERT <sku> price=<new_price_cents>`\n"[39m +
                [32m"  - `action = 'update'` → `UPDATE <sku> price=<old_price_cents>-><new_price_cents>`\n"[39m +
                [32m"  - `action = 'delete'` → `DELETE <sku> price=<old_price_cents>`\n"[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'The type is append-only: inserting is allowed (including directly, by hand), but any attempt to `update` or `delete` an `AuditEvent` must fail with an error whose message contains exactly `AuditEvent is append-only`, and must leave the stored rows unchanged.\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'### 3. `default::AuditBatch` — one row per mutating statement\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'Properties: `kind: str` (required, restricted to exactly `insert`, `update`, `delete`), `row_count: int64` (required), `recorded_at: datetime` (required, defaulting to the time of the statement that created it).\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'Exactly one `AuditBatch` row must be recorded per `insert`/`update`/`delete` statement executed against `Product`, with `kind` naming the statement type and `row_count` holding the number of `Product` objects that statement modified. This includes statements that modified **zero** products (e.g. an `update Product filter ...` whose filter matched nothing): those must still produce exactly one `AuditBatch` row, with `row_count = 0`.\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'### 4. Required declaration names\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'The audit behaviour must be declared in the schema with exactly these names:\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'On `default::Product`:\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'| name | reacts to | granularity |\n'[39m +
                [32m'| --- | --- | --- |\n'[39m +
                [32m'| `log_product_insert` | insert | one `AuditEvent` per inserted product |\n'[39m +
                [32m"| `log_price_update` | update | one `AuditEvent` per updated product, **only** when `price_cents` actually changed — expressed as the trigger declaration's own condition, so the trigger body does not even run otherwise |\n"[39m +
                [32m'| `log_product_delete` | delete | one `AuditEvent` per deleted product |\n'[39m +
                [32m'| `batch_insert_stats` | insert | one `AuditBatch` per statement |\n'[39m +
                [32m'| `batch_update_stats` | update | one `AuditBatch` per statement |\n'[39m +
                [32m'| `batch_delete_stats` | delete | one `AuditBatch` per statement |\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'On `default::AuditEvent`: `forbid_mutation`, reacting to both `update` and `delete`, per row.\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'An `update` of a product that leaves `price_cents` unchanged must therefore produce **no** `AuditEvent` at all (while still bumping `revision` and still producing an `AuditBatch` row).\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'### 5. Migration workflow\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'All of the above must be declared in `dbschema/default.gel` and rolled out through the normal migration workflow, non-interactively. The pre-existing `00001-*.edgeql` migration file must not be edited, renamed or removed, `gel migration status` must report that the database is up to date, and applying your migration must not create any `AuditEvent` or `AuditBatch` rows. All 8 seeded products must still exist afterwards.\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'### 6. Two CLI wrappers\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'Create the following executable scripts (implemented with the `gel` CLI; no client libraries).\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m"`scripts/apply_price_change.sh <sku> <new_price_cents>` — changes one product's price:\n"[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'- On success: exit `0` and print exactly one line to stdout, and nothing else:\n'[39m +
                [32m'  `<sku> <old_price_cents> -> <new_price_cents> revision=<revision after the change>`\n'[39m +
                [32m'  (for example `AX-100 1999 -> 2099 revision=2`). It always performs the update, even when `<new_price_cents>` equals the current price, and it must run exactly one mutating statement per invocation.\n'[39m +
                [32m'- Validation, applied strictly in this order, printing nothing to stdout and leaving the database untouched:\n'[39m +
                [32m'  1. wrong number of arguments → stderr `ERROR: usage: apply_price_change.sh <sku> <new_price_cents>`, exit `4`.\n'[39m +
                [32m'  2. `<new_price_cents>` is not a positive decimal integer (no sign, no leading zero, no decimal point) → stderr `ERROR: invalid price: <the argument as given>`, exit `3`.\n'[39m +
                [32m'  3. no product with that `sku` → stderr `ERROR: unknown sku: <sku>`, exit `2`.\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'`scripts/audit_report.sh` — takes no arguments, always exits `0`, and prints a single JSON array to stdout (whitespace and line breaks inside the JSON do not matter). It contains one object per distinct `sku` that appears in `AuditEvent` — a sku with no audit rows must not appear at all, and an empty audit trail must yield `[]`. Objects are ordered by `sku` ascending and have exactly these six keys:\n'[39m +

                [32m'- `sku` (string)\n'[39m +

                [32m'- `events` (integer): total number of `AuditEvent` rows for that sku\n'[39m +
                [32m"- `net_price_change_cents` (integer): sum of `new_price_cents - old_price_cents` over that sku's `update` rows, `0` when there are none\n"[39m +

        {
          role: [32m'tool'[39m,
          content: [
            {
              type: [32m'tool-result'[39m,
              toolCallId: [32m'KqjiRd2cwqbnxlUI'[39m,
              toolName: [32m'webSearch'[39m,
              output: {
                type: [32m'content'[39m,
                value: [
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# Triggers - Schema | Reference\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2023-03-07, last updated: 2026-07-24, [Read more](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/datamodel/triggers)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Triggers allow you to define an expression to be executed whenever a given\n'[39m +
                      [32m'query type is run on an object type.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'trigger log_update after update for each do (\n'[39m +
                      [32m'insert Log {\n'[39m +
                      [32m"action := 'update',\n"[39m +
                      [32m'target_name := __new__.name,\n'[39m +
                      [32m"change := __old__.name ++ '->' ++ __new__.name\n"[39m +
                      [32m'}\n'[39m +
                      [32m');\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'We can prevent that by\n'[39m +
                      [32m"using the trigger's `when` to run the trigger conditionally.\n"[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'trigger log_update after update for each\n'[39m +
                      [32m'when (__old__.name != __new__.name)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'do (\n'[39m +
                      [32m'insert Log {\n'[39m +
                      [32m"action := 'update',\n"[39m +
                      [32m'target_name := __new__.name,\n'[39m +
                      [32m"change := __old__.name ++ '->' ++ __new__.name\n"[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'trigger log_update after update for each\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'type type-name "{"\n'[39m +
                      [32m'trigger name\n'[39m +
                      [32m'after\n'[39m +
                      [32m'{insert | update | delete} [, ...]\n'[39m +
                      [32m'    for {each | all}\n'[39m +
                      [32m'[ when (condition) ]\n'[39m +
                      [32m'do expr\n'[39m +
                      [32m'"}"\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'{create | alter} type type-name "{"\n'[39m +
                      [32m'create trigger name\n'[39m +
                      [32m'after\n'[39m +
                      [32m'{insert | update | delete} [, ...]\n'[39m +
                      [32m'    for {each | all}\n'[39m +
                      [32m'[ when (condition) ]\n'[39m +
                      [32m'do expr\n'[39m +
                      [32m'"}"'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# EdgeDB 3.0 | Gel Blog\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2023-06-22, last updated: 2026-06-16, [Read more](https://www.geldata.com/blog/edgedb-3-0)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'type Person {\n'[39m +
                      [32m'required name: str;\n'[39m +
                      [32m'trigger log_update after update for each do (\n'[39m +
                      [32m'insert AuditLog {\n'[39m +
                      [32m"action := 'update',\n"[39m +
                      [32m'target_name := __new__.name,\n'[39m +
                      [32m"change := __old__.name ++ '->' ++ __new__.name\n"[39m +
                      [32m'}\n'[39m +
                      [32m');\n'[39m +
                      [32m'}\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'In essence, the distinction between the two is quite straightforward:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'a *Trigger* cannot alter the object that activated it, but it can do pretty much anything else.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'A *Mutation Rewrite*, on the other hand, enables you to intercept mutating queries and rewrite them conditionally based on the old or new value, or even on what was specified precisely in the mutating query.\n'[39m +
                      [32m"To put it in SQL terms, EdgeDB's mutation rewrites correspond to SQL's `before` triggers, while EdgeDB's triggers align with SQL's\n"[39m +
                      [32m'`after` triggers.'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# Link property challenges · geldata gel · Discussion #8492\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2025-03-20, last updated: 2026-05-29, [Read more](https://github.com/geldata/gel/discussions/8492)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m''[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual :: 27.3 Using Triggers\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: undefined, last updated: 2026-05-31, [Read more](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/triggers.html)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'A trigger is defined to activate when a statement inserts, updates,\n'[39m +
                      [32m'or deletes rows in the associated table.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'These row operations are\n'[39m +
                      [32m'trigger events.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'For example, rows can be inserted by\n'[39m +
                      [32m'`INSERT` or `LOAD\n'[39m +
                      [32m'DATA` statements, and an insert trigger activates for each inserted row.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'A trigger can be set to activate either before or after the trigger event.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'For example, you can have a trigger activate before each row that is inserted into a table or after each row that is updated.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Important\n'[39m +
                      [32m'MySQL triggers activate only for changes made to tables by SQL\n'[39m +
                      [32m'statements.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'This includes changes to base tables that underlie\n'[39m +
                      [32m'updatable views.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Triggers do not activate for changes to tables\n'[39m +
                      [32m'made by APIs that do not transmit SQL statements to the MySQL\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Server.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'This means that triggers are not activated by updates made\n'[39m +
                      [32m'using the `NDB` API.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Triggers are not activated by changes in\n'[39m +
                      [32m'`INFORMATION_SCHEMA` or\n'[39m +
                      [32m'`performance_schema` tables.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Those tables are\n'[39m +
                      [32m'actually views and triggers are not permitted on views.'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# Triggers - Introspection - Schema | Reference - Gel Docs\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: undefined, last updated: 2026-06-16, [Read more](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/datamodel/introspection/triggers)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Introspection of a trigger named `log_insert` on the `User` type:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Copy\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'with module schema\n'[39m +
                      [32m'select Trigger {\n'[39m +
                      [32m'name,\n'[39m +
                      [32m'kinds,\n'[39m +
                      [32m'timing,\n'[39m +
                      [32m'scope,\n'[39m +
                      [32m'expr,\n'[39m +
                      [32m'subject: {\n'[39m +
                      [32m'name\n'[39m +
                      [32m'}\n'[39m +
                      [32m"} filter .name = 'log_insert';\n"[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'{\n'[39m +
                      [32m'schema::Trigger {\n'[39m +
                      [32m"name: 'log_insert',\n"[39m +
                      [32m'kinds: {Insert},\n'[39m +
                      [32m'timing: After,\n'[39m +
                      [32m'scope: Each,\n'[39m +
                      [32m"expr: 'insert default::Log { action := \\'insert\\', target_name := __new__.name }',\n"[39m +
                      [32m"subject: schema::ObjectType {name: 'default::User'},\n"[39m +
                      [32m'},\n'[39m +
                      [32m'}\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'︙'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# 27.3.1 Trigger Syntax and Examples\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: undefined, last updated: 2026-07-27, [Read more](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/trigger-syntax.html)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- The keyword `BEFORE` indicates the trigger\n'[39m +
                      [32m'action time.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'In this case, the trigger activates before each\n'[39m +
                      [32m'row inserted into the table.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'The other permitted keyword here\n'[39m +
                      [32m'is `AFTER`.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'that also has the same trigger event and action time.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'In an `UPDATE`\n'[39m +
                      [32m'trigger, you can use\n'[39m +
                      [32m'`OLD.*`col_name`*` to\n'[39m +
                      [32m'refer to the columns of a row before it is updated and\n'[39m +
                      [32m'`NEW.*`col_name`*` to\n'[39m +
                      [32m'refer to the columns of the row after it is updated.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'with `SET NEW.*`col_name`* =\n'[39m +
                      [32m'*`value`*` if you have the\n'[39m +
                      [32m'`UPDATE` privilege for it.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'This means you can use a trigger to modify the values to be inserted into a new row or used to update a row.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'(Such a `SET`\n'[39m +
                      [32m'statement has no effect in an `AFTER` trigger\n'[39m +
                      [32m'because the row change has already occurred.)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- An `AFTER` trigger is executed only if any\n'[39m +
                      [32m'`BEFORE` triggers and the row operation\n'[39m +
                      [32m'execute successfully.'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m"# MySQL AFTER UPDATE Trigger - A Beginner's Guide\n"[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2022-02-28, last updated: 2025-10-18, [Read more](https://mysqlcode.com/mysql-after-update-trigger/)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'The AFTER UPDATE trigger activates after the UPDATE query is fired on the table.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'As soon as the data in the table gets modified by the UPDATE query, the trigger body executes and does its work.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'It is nearly the same as the BEFORE UPDATE trigger but it activates after the data is modified in the table.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Therefore, you can not modify the new values as well as the old values that are to be updated.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'However, you can access the new and old values using NEW and OLD keywords.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Following are the restrictions on the AFTER UPDATE trigger.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- You can access the OLD values but can not modify them.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- You can access the NEW values but can not modify them.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- You cannot create the AFTER UPDATE trigger for views.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'…\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'CREATE TRIGGER trigger_name\n'[39m +
                      [32m'AFTER UPDATE\n'[39m +
                      [32m'ON table_name FOR EACH ROW\n'[39m +
                      [32m'[trigger_order]\n'[39m +
                      [32m'BEGIN\n'[39m +
                      [32m'trigger_body\n'[39m +
                      [32m'END\n'[39m +
                      [32m'DELIMITER ;\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'CREATE TRIGGER after_update\n'[39m +
                      [32m'AFTER UPDATE ON prod_details\n'[39m +
                      [32m'FOR EACH ROW\n'[39m +
                      [32m'BEGIN\n'[39m +
                      [32m'IF OLD.quantity!=NEW.quantity THEN\n'[39m +
                      [32m'INSERT INTO q_details(prod_id,old_q,new_q,updated_at)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'VALUES(OLD.id,OLD.quantity,NEW.quantity, NOW());\n'[39m +
                      [32m'END IF;\n'[39m +
                      [32m'END\n'[39m +
                      [32m'//'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# SQL Trigger Update: After Update & SQL Server\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2024-10-30, last updated: 2026-05-01, [Read more](https://www.studysmarter.co.uk/explanations/computer-science/databases/sql-trigger-update/)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'In SQL Server, creating a trigger requires defining the trigger body and specifying the **AFTER** or **INSTEAD OF** actions:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- **AFTER Trigger:** Executes after the update operation, making it suitable for scenarios where data must be validated or logged after changes.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'The **SQL Server Trigger After Update** is an essential component that automatically executes specified actions following an update operation on a given table.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'This means once a record is modified, the trigger will initiate without any further prompting.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'This behavior enhances data integrity and visibility regarding changes that occur in the database.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Triggers can be used to log changes, enforce business rules, or even update other tables accordingly.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'CREATE TRIGGER trigger_name ON table_name AFTER UPDATE AS BEGIN -- SQL statements END\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- In SQL Server, triggers can be defined as **AFTER** or **INSTEAD OF** triggers, enabling specific actions either after an update has occurred or overriding the update process entirely.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'BEFORE triggers are executed before the actual update occurs, allowing for validation or modification of data before it is committed.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'AFTER triggers run after the update has been completed, typically for actions like logging or cascading changes.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Both can prevent or signal an update, but at different execution times.'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Triggers - Depesz\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2012-11-14, last updated: 2026-06-25, [Read more](https://www.depesz.com/2012/11/14/how-i-learned-to-stop-worrying-and-love-the-triggers/)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m"Let's consider it in case of UPDATE.\n"[39m +
                      [32m"You're running an update.\n"[39m +
                      [32m"PostgreSQL has to check that all values you provided are sensible, match all constraints (not null, checks, unique), then it actually updates the row (well, technically it doesn't because PostgreSQL has mvcc, but for now let's pretend that it does).\n"[39m +
                      [32m'BEFORE trigger is called just before the internal row representation is updated.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'AFTER trigger is called afterwards.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'For starters – if you want to modify new values inserted/updated to the table – the correct place to do it is in BEFORE trigger.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'I have seen code, where people were adding AFTER INSERT trigger, which issued UPDATE of newly inserted record.\n'[39m +
                      [32m"That just doesn't make sense.\n"[39m +
                      [32m'It bloats the table, and is slower.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'In BEFORE trigger, you can modify the row data before it will be stored in table.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'AFTER triggers are meant to be place where you put logic that influences other tables when the modifiation of your original table succeds.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Hence – if you have to issue insert/update/delete from trigger – it should *almost always* be AFTER trigger.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'And then it sets last_modified to now().'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# Documentation: 8.0: Triggers\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2012-01-01, last updated: 2026-06-10, [Read more](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/8.0/triggers.html)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'A trigger can be defined to execute before or after an\n'[39m +
                      [32m'INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE operation, either once per modified row, or once per SQL statement.\n'[39m +
                      [32m"If a trigger event occurs, the trigger's function is called at the appropriate time to handle the event.\n"[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Statement-level "before" triggers naturally fire before the statement starts to do anything, while statement-level "after" triggers fire at the very end of the statement.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Row-level "before" triggers fire immediately before a particular row is operated on, while row-level "after" triggers fire at the end of the statement (but before any statement-level "after" triggers).\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'The return value is ignored for row-level triggers fired\n'[39m +
                      [32m'after an operation, and so they may as well return NULL.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Typically, row before triggers are used for checking or\n'[39m +
                      [32m'modifying the data that will be inserted or updated.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'For\n'[39m +
                      [32m'example, a before trigger might be used to insert the current\n'[39m +
                      [32m'time into a timestamp column, or to check that two elements of\n'[39m +
                      [32m'the row are consistent.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Row after triggers are most sensibly\n'[39m +
                      [32m'used to propagate the updates to other tables, or make\n'[39m +
                      [32m'…'[39m
                  }
                ]
              },
              providerOptions: {
                vertex: {
                  thoughtSignature: [32m''[39m
                }
              }
            }
          ]

                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m`I'm currently investigating Gel's "Mutation Rewrite" concept. It appears to allow conditional interception and modification of mutating queries, taking into account both old and new values.\n`[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m''[39m
            },

        {
          role: [32m'tool'[39m,
          content: [
            {
              type: [32m'tool-result'[39m,
              toolCallId: [32m'dvsSsXQQtIbTiwh1'[39m,
              toolName: [32m'webSearch'[39m,
              output: {
                type: [32m'content'[39m,
                value: [
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# Mutation rewrites\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2024-01-01, last updated: 2025-01-11, [Read more](https://docs.edgedb.com/database/reference/sdl/mutation_rewrites)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Declare two mutation rewrites: one that sets a\n'[39m +
                      [32m'`created` property when a new\n'[39m +
                      [32m'object is inserted and one that sets a\n'[39m +
                      [32m'`modified` property on each update:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: datetime {\n'[39m +
                      [32m'rewrite insert using (datetime_of_statement());\n'[39m +
                      [32m'modified: datetime {\n'[39m +
                      [32m'rewrite update using (datetime_of_statement());\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'## Syntax\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Define a new mutation rewrite corresponding to the more explicit DDL commands.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'rewrite {insert | update} [, ...]\n'[39m +
                      [32m'using expr\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Mutation rewrites must be defined inside a property or link block.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'This declaration defines a new trigger with the following options:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- insert | update [, ...]\n'[39m +
                      [32m'The query type (or types) the rewrite runs on.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Separate multiple values with commas to invoke the same rewrite for multiple types of queries.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- expr\n'[39m +
                      [32m'The expression to be evaluated to produce the new value of the property.'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# EdgeDB 3.0 | Gel Blog\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2023-06-22, last updated: 2026-06-16, [Read more](https://www.geldata.com/blog/edgedb-3-0)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- *Triggers* and *mutation rewrites* let you implement advanced validation and make the database *react* to your queries in interesting ways.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'The result?\n'[39m +
                      [32m'EdgeQL got two new mechanisms: "Triggers" and "Mutation Rewrites".\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'In essence, the distinction between the two is quite straightforward:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'a *Trigger* cannot alter the object that activated it, but it can do pretty much anything else.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'A *Mutation Rewrite*, on the other hand, enables you to intercept mutating queries and rewrite them conditionally based on the old or new value, or even on what was specified precisely in the mutating query.\n'[39m +
                      [32m"To put it in SQL terms, EdgeDB's mutation rewrites correspond to SQL's `before` triggers, while EdgeDB's triggers align with SQL's\n"[39m +
                      [32m'`after` triggers.'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# Mutation rewrites - Schema | Reference\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2023-04-05, last updated: 2026-06-13, [Read more](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/datamodel/mutation_rewrites)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Mutation rewrites allow you to intercept database mutations (i.e.,\n'[39m +
                      [32m'inserts and/or updates) and set the value of a property or link to the result of an expression you define.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'They can be defined in your schema.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Mutation rewrites are complementary to triggers.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'rewrite {insert | update} [, ...]\n'[39m +
                      [32m'  using expr\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'When creating a new property or link:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'{create | alter} type type-name "{"\n'[39m +
                      [32m'create { property | link } prop-or-link-name: type "{"\n'[39m +
                      [32m'create rewrite {insert | update} [, ...]\n'[39m +
                      [32m'      using expr\n'[39m +
                      [32m'"}" ;\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'When altering an existing property or link:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'{create | alter} type type-name "{"\n'[39m +
                      [32m'alter { property | link } prop-or-link-name "{"\n'[39m +
                      [32m'create rewrite {insert | update} [, ...]\n'[39m +
                      [32m'      using expr\n'[39m +
                      [32m'"}" ;\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'The command `create rewrite` nested under `create type` or `alter type`\n'[39m +
                      [32m'and then under `create property/link` or `alter property/link` defines a\n'[39m +
                      [32m'new mutation rewrite for the given property or link on the given object.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- **insert | update [, ...]**\n'[39m +
                      [32m'The query type (or types) that are rewritten.'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# Using a mutation rewrite as a better property default in the ...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2025-01-29, last updated: 2025-10-03, [Read more](https://miroslavpetrik.medium.com/using-a-mutation-rewrite-as-a-better-default-property-in-the-edgedb-1c81b660368f)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'A more powerful construct which allows us to hook into the database mutations are the mutation rewrites.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Since we want to set the initial value, we can use the\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'insert\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'rewrite:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'type Reservation { required price: float32 { rewrite insert using (.room.price * .daysCount); }}\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Finally this gets the job done, but there is a catch — the\n'[39m +
                      [32m'…\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'When we attempt to insert an Reservation, the client (CLI, or TypeScript) will require the\n'[39m +
                      [32m'…\n'[39m +
                      [32m'property, even though it will always get overwritten with the mutation rewrite:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'import e from "@/src/edgeql-js";e.insert(e.Reservation, {price: 0 /* The value is required, but unused! */});\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'We can update the rewrite, so when an initial price is set in the insert query, it will be used instead of the computed value:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'type Reservation { price: float32 { rewrite insert using (__subject__.price ?? (.room.price * .daysCount)); }}\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Note, that here we need to make the\n'[39m +
                      [32m'…\n'[39m +
                      [32m'property optional, so the client won’t require the price property.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'rewrite insert\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'.'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# EdgeDB 3.0 Mutation Rewrites & Triggers- Audit logs, cached computeds, super constraints, and more!\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2023-07-04, last updated: 2026-02-12, [Read more](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ImgMfb_jCJQ)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Mutation rewrites and triggers are two complementary EdgeDB 3.0 features with tons of different uses.\n'[39m +
                      [32m"Your database does stuff for you so your application doesn't have to!\n"[39m +
                      [32m'🤖 Track when an object is updated in a property on that same object with mutation rewrites\n'[39m +
                      [32m'🤖 Create detailed audit log records using triggers\n'[39m +
                      [32m'🤖 Mutate values as they come into your database with mutation rewrites\n'[39m +
                      [32m'🤖 Make more flexible constraints by pairing triggers with the `assert` function\n'[39m +
                      [32m'🤖 Cache computed values with mutation rewrites\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'• Mutation rewrites- https://www.edgedb.com/docs/datamodel/mutation_rewrites\n'[39m +
                      [32m'• Triggers- https://www.edgedb.com/docs/datamodel/triggers\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'{ts:21} by adding a mutation rewrite I can update the value automatically every time the object is mutated'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# GitHub - geldata/rfcs: RFCs for major changes to EdgeDB\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2020-01-28, last updated: 2026-04-17, [Read more](https://github.com/geldata/rfcs)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- RFC 1020 - Triggers (accepted)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- RFC 1021 - Mutation rewrites (accepted)'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# v4.0 - Changelog | Resources\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: undefined, last updated: 2026-03-12, [Read more](https://docs.geldata.com/resources/changelog/4_x)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'3. Take your application offline, then dump your v3.x database with the CLI\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Copy\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'$\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'gel dump --dsn <old dsn> --all --format dir my_database.dump/\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'…\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'gel restore --all my_database.dump/ --dsn <new dsn>\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'…\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- Type check mutation rewrites at migration time\n'[39m +
                      [32m'(#6466)\n'[39m +
                      [32m"Mutation rewrite's `using` expression are now required to be of correct\n"[39m +
                      [32m'type when the rewrite is created.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Up until now, it was possible to migrate to\n'[39m +
                      [32m'a schema that contained a rewrite rule that would always throw a type error\n'[39m +
                      [32m'when an object was being inserted or updated.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'This might be considered a breaking change, but as it is clearly a bug in\n'[39m +
                      [32m'user schema and as it could also be considered a bug in the compiler, we are\n'[39m +
                      [32m'fixing it in a minor version.'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# Mutation rewrites - Introspection - Schema | Reference\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: undefined, last updated: 2026-06-13, [Read more](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/datamodel/introspection/mutation_rewrites)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'select schema::ObjectType {\n'[39m +
                      [32m'name,\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'properties: {\n'[39m +
                      [32m'name\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m"} filter .name = 'schema::Rewrite';\n"[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m"name: 'schema::Rewrite',\n"[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Introspection of all properties in the `default` schema with a mutation\n'[39m +
                      [32m'rewrite:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'select schema::ObjectType {\n'[39m +
                      [32m'name,\n'[39m +
                      [32m'properties := (\n'[39m +
                      [32m'select .properties {\n'[39m +
                      [32m'name,\n'[39m +
                      [32m'rewrites: {\n'[39m +
                      [32m'kind\n'[39m +
                      [32m'}\n'[39m +
                      [32m'} filter exists .rewrites\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m"} filter .name ilike 'default::%'\n"[39m +
                      [32m'and exists .properties.rewrites;\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Introspection of all rewrites, including the type of query (`kind`),\n'[39m +
                      [32m'rewrite expression, and the object and property they are on:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'select schema::Rewrite {\n'[39m +
                      [32m'subject := (\n'[39m +
                      [32m'select .subject {\n'[39m +
                      [32m'name,\n'[39m +
                      [32m'source: {\n'[39m +
                      [32m'name\n'[39m +
                      [32m'}\n'[39m +
                      [32m'}\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'kind,\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'`modified`:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Copy\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'db>...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'select schema::Rewrite {kind, expr}\n'[39m +
                      [32m"filter .subject.source.name = 'default::Post'\n"[39m +
                      [32m"and .subject.name = 'modified';\n"[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'schema::Rewrite {\n'[39m +
                      [32m'kind: Insert,\n'[39m +
                      [32m"expr: 'std::datetime_of_statement()'\n"[39m +
                      [32m'},\n'[39m +
                      [32m'schema::Rewrite {\n'[39m +
                      [32m'kind: Update,\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'}'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# Feature-Request: Query/Mutation Hook Support · geldata gel · Discussion #3455\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2022-02-11, last updated: 2026-04-16, [Read more](https://github.com/geldata/gel/discussions/3455)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'# Feature-Request: Query/Mutation Hook Support #3455\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'## Mutation Hooks\n'[39m +
                      [32m'These hooks will trigger on insert/update/delete.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'**They should also be able to modify/extend the users intentions by returning data to EdgeDB**\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Following hooks will be needed to cover the mutation side of things:\n'[39m +

                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# Mutation rewrites - Schema | Reference\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2023-04-05, last updated: 2026-06-13, [Read more](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/datamodel/mutation_rewrites)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Mutation rewrites allow you to intercept database mutations (i.e.,\n'[39m +
                      [32m'inserts and/or updates) and set the value of a property or link to the result of an expression you define.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'They can be defined in your schema.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'}\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Copy\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'type Post {\n'[39m +
                      [32m'required title: str;\n'[39m +
                      [32m'required body: str;\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: datetime {\n'[39m +
                      [32m'rewrite insert using (datetime_of_statement())\n'[39m +
                      [32m'}\n'[39m +
                      [32m'modified: datetime {\n'[39m +
                      [32m'rewrite update using (datetime_of_statement())\n'[39m +

                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Define a new mutation rewrite corresponding to the more explicit DDL commands.\n'[39m +

                      [32m'rewrite {insert | update} [, ...]\n'[39m +

                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# Managing Mutations in ClickHouse\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2026-03-03, last updated: 2026-07-15, [Read more](https://bigdataboutique.com/blog/clickhouse-managing-mutations)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'In ClickHouse, a mutation is any operation that logically modifies existing data in a MergeTree table.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'The two most common triggers are:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- `ALTER TABLE ...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'UPDATE` - modifying values in existing rows\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- `ALTER TABLE ...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'DELETE` - removing rows that match a condition\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Because MergeTree data parts are immutable, ClickHouse cannot modify them in place.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Instead, a mutation rewrites every affected part, producing new versions with the changes applied.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'In many conditions, this means a **full table rewrite** - every part in the table gets read, transformed, and written back to disk.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'For large data transformations - changing column types, restructuring data, or applying complex updates - consider the insert-select-rename pattern instead of a mutation.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'The approach is:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'1. Create a new table with the desired schema or structure.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'2. `INSERT INTO new_table SELECT ...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'FROM old_table` with the transformations applied in the SELECT.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'3. Rename the old table to a backup name and rename the new table to the original name.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- Mutations (ALTER TABLE UPDATE/DELETE) rewrite data parts and can mean a full table rewrite.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'They are far more expensive than equivalent operations in row-store databases.'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# EdgeDB 3.0 Mutation Rewrites & Triggers- Audit logs, cached ...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2023-07-04, last updated: 2026-02-12, [Read more](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ImgMfb_jCJQ)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Mutation rewrites and triggers are two complementary EdgeDB 3.0 features with tons of different uses.\n'[39m +
                      [32m"Your database does stuff for you so your application doesn't have to!\n"[39m +
                      [32m'🤖 Track when an object is updated in a property on that same object with mutation rewrites\n'[39m +
                      [32m'🤖 Create detailed audit log records using triggers\n'[39m +
                      [32m'🤖 Mutate values as they come into your database with mutation rewrites\n'[39m +
                      [32m'🤖 Make more flexible constraints by pairing triggers with the `assert` function\n'[39m +
                      [32m'🤖 Cache computed values with mutation rewrites\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'{ts:21} by adding a mutation rewrite I can update the value automatically every time the object is mutated\n'[39m +
                      [32m"{ts:27} I'm going to insert a new user and select it so you can see the last updated value\n"[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'{ts:41} if I want even more detailed logging it might make sense to create a log type and insert a new one each time my\n'[39m +
                      [32m'{ts:49} objects are mutated this trigger will do just that it will write a log object with a link'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# WL#8776: Query Rewrite Plugin: Support insert, update and delete statements\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: undefined, last updated: 2026-03-26, [Read more](https://dev.mysql.com/worklog/task/?id=8776)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- F1: The plugin shall accept any form of INSERT statement, with support for parameter markers, for its pattern and match it to identical incoming queries.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- F2: The plugin shall accept any form of UPDATE statement, with support for parameter markers, for its pattern and match it to identical incoming queries.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- F3: The plugin shall accept any form of DELETE statement, with support for parameter markers, for its pattern and match it to identical incoming queries.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'To use INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements in the Rewriter plugin the user has to specify such a statement in the rule table.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'This is done by inserting rules into the Rewriters table named rewrite_rules.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'This works just like it does for SELECT statements; the user must specify a pattern and a replacement in order to create a rewrite rule.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'The pattern and the replacement does not have to be of the same type, for example the following rule is valid:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'> Pattern:DELETE FROM t1 WHERE col = ?Replacement:UPDATE t1 SET col = NULL WHERE col = ?\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'The only functional change done to the Rewriter plugin was that the check that accepts the statement type was expanded to allow INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements.'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# 7.6.4 The Rewriter Query Rewrite Plugin\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2025-08-03, last updated: 2026-01-20, [Read more](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/9.6/en/rewriter-query-rewrite-plugin.html)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'A server-side plugin named\n'[39m +
                      [32m'`Rewriter`examines statements and may rewrite them, based on its in-memory cache of rewrite rules.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'These statements are subject to rewriting:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'`SELECT`,\n'[39m +
                      [32m'`INSERT`,\n'[39m +
                      [32m'`REPLACE`,\n'[39m +
                      [32m'`UPDATE`, and\n'[39m +
                      [32m'`DELETE`.'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# Rewriting MySQL queries on the fly\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2025-09-09, last updated: 2025-09-22, [Read more](https://www.galliumdata.com/use-cases/rewriting-mysql-queries-on-the-fly)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'The most commonly available implementation of these rewrite plugins is the Rewriter plugin, which can modify incoming queries such as SELECT, UPDATE and so on.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'This plugin allows you to substitute certain SQL queries for others using a lookup table.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Before MySQL 8.0.12, it only worked with SELECT statements, but since then it also works with INSERT, REPLACE, UPDATE and DELETE (but nothing else -- no DDL, no SET, CALL, etc...)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'You create a new replacement rule by simply inserting a row into the rewrite_rules table:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'INSERT INTO query_rewrite.rewrite_rules ( pattern, replacement )\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m"Whenever you install (or remove) a rule, you need to flush it because they're held in memory:\n"[39m +
                      [32m'CALL query_rewrite.flush_rewrite_rules()\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Once the plugin is installed and active in MySQL, and the substitution rule is in place, then any time someone executes the following query:\n'[39m +
                      [32m"select id, name, dob from mydb.customers where name = 'Adam'\n"[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'There are no real limitations to the replacement query, but it must be a single statement.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'For instance, you could substitute an UPDATE statement for a DELETE statement, if that makes sense in your particular scenario.'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# Iceberg tables INSERT, MERGE, and DELETE Operations\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2026-08-02, last updated: 2026-07-13, [Read more](https://iomete.com/resources/reference/iceberg-tables/writes)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'**IOMETE** supports `INSERT INTO`, `MERGE INTO`, and `INSERT OVERWRITE`\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'To append new data to a table, use `INSERT INTO`.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'`MERGE INTO` queries that can express row-level updates.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Iceberg supports `MERGE INTO` by rewriting data files that contain rows that need to be updated in an `overwrite` commit.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'**MERGE INTO is recommended instead of INSERT OVERWRITE** because Iceberg can replace only the affected data files, and because the data overwritten by a dynamic overwrite may change if the table’s partitioning changes.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'`MERGE INTO` updates a table, called the target table, using a set of updates from another query, called the source.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'The update for a row in the target table is found using the `ON` clause that is like a join condition.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'MERGE INTO db.target t -- a target table\n'[39m +
                      [32m'USING (SELECT ...) s -- the source updates\n'[39m +
                      [32m'ON t.id = s.id -- condition to find updates for target rows\n'[39m +
                      [32m'WHEN ...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'-- updates\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'`INSERT OVERWRITE` can replace data in the table with the result of a query.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Overwrites are atomic operations for Iceberg tables.'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# Backfill Columns Using ALTER/UPDATE with Dictionary Lookups\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2026-06-10, last updated: 2026-06-15, [Read more](https://pulse.support/kb/clickhouse-backfill-column-with-dictionary-lookup)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'### 1.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Create the lookup dictionary\n'[39m +
                      [32m"The dictionary's source is the table that holds the values you want to write.\n"[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'### 2.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Run the backfill mutation\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Use\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'|One-off correction|Good — arbitrary expression, no schema change to the column|Requires the expression to live in the schema|\n'[39m +
                      [32m'|Mechanism|Mutation (rewrites affected parts)|Mutation (rewrites the column for existing parts)|\n'[39m +
                      [32m"|Best for|Backfilling a value that won't be recomputed going forward|A derived column you want populated for old and future rows|\n"[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'2. **Filter with** Only rewrite rows you actually have a value for; leave the rest untouched.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'**Q: Will the backfill auto-populate new inserts going forward?**\n'[39m +
                      [32m'No. An\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'ALTER ... UPDATE\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'mutation only touches existing data. For continuous population, either supply the value at insert time, use a\n'[39m +
                      [32m'…\n'[39m +
                      [32m'column, or enrich at query time. See dictionary-driven updates for those patterns.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'**Q: Can I avoid overwriting rows that have no matching key?**\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Yes. Add\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m"WHERE dictHas('dict', key)\n"[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'so only rows with a match are rewritten, or use'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# How to Use Lightweight UPDATE in ClickHouse\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2026-03-31, last updated: 2026-07-13, [Read more](https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-03-31-clickhouse-lightweight-update/view)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'ClickHouse has historically handled updates through heavy mutations that asynchronously rewrite entire data parts.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Starting with newer versions, ClickHouse supports a lighter `UPDATE` approach that complements lightweight DELETE.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Before lightweight updates, the only option was `ALTER TABLE ...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'UPDATE`:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'ALTER TABLE orders\n'[39m +
                      [32m"UPDATE status = 'shipped'\n"[39m +
                      [32m'WHERE order_id = 12345;\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'This is a mutation - it is asynchronous and rewrites the affected data parts in the background.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'ClickHouse now supports standard `UPDATE` DML:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'UPDATE orders\n'[39m +
                      [32m"SET status = 'shipped', updated_at = now()\n"[39m +
                      [32m'WHERE order_id = 12345;\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Lightweight UPDATE in ClickHouse brings standard SQL DML syntax using patch parts rather than full mutation rewrites.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'For high-frequency state changes, consider append-based design with `ReplacingMergeTree`.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'For occasional corrections or bulk updates, the `UPDATE` statement is the cleanest approach.'[39m
                  }
                ]

                    text: [32m'# Mutation rewrites - Schema | Reference\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2023-04-05, last updated: 2026-06-13, [Read more](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/datamodel/mutation_rewrites)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Mutation rewrites allow you to intercept database mutations (i.e.,\n'[39m +
                      [32m'inserts and/or updates) and set the value of a property or link to the result of an expression you define.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'They can be defined in your schema.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m"Inside the rewrite rule's expression, you have access to a few special values:\n"[39m +
                      [32m'- `__subject__` refers to the object type with the new property and link\n'[39m +
                      [32m'values.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- `__specified__` is a named tuple with a key for each property or link in\n'[39m +
                      [32m'the type and a boolean value indicating whether this value was explicitly set\n'[39m +
                      [32m'in the mutation.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- `__old__` refers to the object type with the previous property and link\n'[39m +
                      [32m'values (available for update-only mutation rewrites).\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'      using expr\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'The command `create rewrite` nested under `create type` or `alter type`\n'[39m +
                      [32m'and then under `create property/link` or `alter property/link` defines a\n'[39m +
                      [32m'new mutation rewrite for the given property or link on the given object.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- **prop-or-link-name**\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- **insert | update [, ...]**\n'[39m +
                      [32m'The query type (or types) that are rewritten.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Separate multiple values with commas to invoke the same rewrite for multiple types of queries.'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# EdgeDB 3.0 | Gel Blog\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2023-06-22, last updated: 2026-06-16, [Read more](https://www.geldata.com/blog/edgedb-3-0)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'In essence, the distinction between the two is quite straightforward:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'a *Trigger* cannot alter the object that activated it, but it can do pretty much anything else.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'A *Mutation Rewrite*, on the other hand, enables you to intercept mutating queries and rewrite them conditionally based on the old or new value, or even on what was specified precisely in the mutating query.\n'[39m +
                      [32m"To put it in SQL terms, EdgeDB's mutation rewrites correspond to SQL's `before` triggers, while EdgeDB's triggers align with SQL's\n"[39m +
                      [32m'`after` triggers.'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# Gel: docs/reference/datamodel/triggers.rst | Fossies\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: 2023-03-07, last updated: 2026-03-29, [Read more](https://fossies.org/linux/gel/docs/reference/datamodel/triggers.rst)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Triggers cannot be used to *modify* the object that set off the trigger, although they can be used with `assert` to do\n'[39m +
                      [32m'*validation* on that object.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'If you need to modify the object, you can use `mutation\n'[39m +
                      [32m'rewrites <ref_datamodel_mutation_rewrites>`.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m"In a trigger's expression, we have access to the `__old__`\n"[39m +
                      [32m'and/or `__new__` variables which capture the object before\n'[39m +
                      [32m'and after the query.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Triggers on `update` can use both\n'[39m +
                      [32m'variables.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Triggers on `delete` can use `__old__`.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Triggers on `insert` can use `__new__`.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'> "}"\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Optionally provide a condition for the trigger.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'If the condition is met, the trigger will run.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'If not, the trigger is skipped.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'- **`<expr>`**\n'[39m +
                      [32m'The expression to be evaluated when the trigger is invoked.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'> - **{create | alter} type <type-name> "{"**\n'[39m +
                      [32m'>   - **create trigger <name>** after {insert | update | delete} [, ...] for {each | all} [ when (<condition>) ] do <expr>\n'[39m +
                      [32m'> "}"'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# Mutation rewrites - Introspection - Schema | Reference - Gel Docs\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: undefined, last updated: 2026-06-13, [Read more](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/datamodel/introspection/mutation_rewrites)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Introspection of all rewrites, including the type of query (`kind`),\n'[39m +
                      [32m'rewrite expression, and the object and property they are on:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Copy\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'select schema::Rewrite {\n'[39m +
                      [32m'subject := (\n'[39m +
                      [32m'select .subject {\n'[39m +
                      [32m'name,\n'[39m +
                      [32m'source: {\n'[39m +
                      [32m'name\n'[39m +
                      [32m'}\n'[39m +
                      [32m'}\n'[39m +
                      [32m'),\n'[39m +
                      [32m'kind,\n'[39m +
                      [32m'expr\n'[39m +
                      [32m'};\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Introspection of all rewrites on a `default::Post` property named\n'[39m +
                      [32m'`modified`:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'db>...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'select schema::Rewrite {kind, expr}\n'[39m +
                      [32m"filter .subject.source.name = 'default::Post'\n"[39m +
                      [32m"and .subject.name = 'modified';\n"[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'{\n'[39m +
                      [32m'schema::Rewrite {\n'[39m +
                      [32m'kind: Insert,\n'[39m +
                      [32m"expr: 'std::datetime_of_statement()'\n"[39m +
                      [32m'},\n'[39m +
                      [32m'schema::Rewrite {\n'[39m +
                      [32m'kind: Update,\n'[39m +
                      [32m"expr: 'std::datetime_of_statement()'\n"[39m +
                      [32m'}\n'[39m +
                      [32m'}\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'︙'[39m
                  },
                  {
                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# v4.0 - Changelog | Resources\n'[39m +

                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m"Mutation rewrite's `using` expression are now required to be of correct\n"[39m +

                      [32m'Up until now, it was possible to migrate to\n'[39m +

                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# Mutations - GraphQL - Using Gel | Reference\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: undefined, last updated: 2026-05-29, [Read more](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/using/graphql/mutations)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Gel provides GraphQL mutations to perform `delete`, `insert`\n'[39m +
                      [32m'and `update` operations.\n'[39m +
                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m'|GraphQL|EdgeQL equivalent|'[39m

                    type: [32m'text'[39m,
                    text: [32m'# Introspection - Schema | Reference - Gel Docs\n'[39m +
                      [32m'created: undefined, last updated: 2026-06-25, [Read more](https://docs.geldata.com/reference/datamodel/introspection)\n'[39m +
                      [32m'\n'[39m +
                      [32m'The following query will give a list of all the types used in introspection:\n'[39m +
                      [32m'Copy\n'[39m +
                      [32m'```\n'[39m +
                      [32m'select name := schema::ObjectType.name\n'[39m +

                      [32m'...\n'[39m +
                      [32m"There's also a couple of ways of getting the introspection type of a\n"[39m +

                      [32m'Any `Object` has a `__type__` link\n'[39m +
